prompt: In many societies, a growing number of older people live alone and have little regular contact with others. What are the causes of this isolation, and what could be done to reduce it?
essay:
The number of older people living alone has risen steadily across most wealthy societies, and a significant proportion of them report going several days at a time without speaking to anyone. The causes are partly demographic and partly a matter of how daily life has been reorganised.

The demographic element is straightforward. People live considerably longer than they once did, often outliving a partner by a decade or more, while adult children increasingly move for work rather than remaining in the same town. A parent who would once have aged surrounded by relatives now frequently ages several hours away from the nearest one.

The less obvious cause is the loss of unplanned contact. Much of an ordinary person's social life is not arranged but incidental: colleagues, a familiar shopkeeper, other parents at a school gate. Retirement removes the first of these at a stroke, and the gradual replacement of local shops and services by out-of-town or online alternatives removes many of the rest. What is left has to be deliberately organised, and organising social contact requires energy and confidence that isolation itself steadily erodes.

Useful responses therefore need to rebuild incidental contact rather than schedule it. Shared community facilities within walking distance — a library, a café, a garden — create the low-stakes repeated encounters that friendship actually grows from, in a way that a weekly organised visit does not. Transport matters for the same reason, since an older person who cannot easily leave the house is dependent on others coming to them. Volunteer befriending schemes have value, though they treat the symptom rather than the design fault that produced it.
title: Loneliness among older people
